findings.title: Denial cache key collides across identities
findings.body: Check builds the new denial-cache key from the raw subject id only (namespace, user UID, action, name, folder) and never includes the identity type or the resolved user UID. Anonymous and render subjects are both "…:0", so they share one key, and a hit returns Allowed=false before renderer or anonymous permissions are evaluated. A denied anonymous dashboards:read Check therefore makes the image renderer, which is hard-coded to be allowed dashboards:read and folders:read, get Allowed=false for that same name and folder for shortCacheTTL (30s). Repeating the anonymous check keeps rendering broken. The same raw id also conflates subject forms this service otherwise treats as distinct, such as a numeric user id versus a UID string.

findings.title: Undelimited denial key collides across resources
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name, and parent with underscores and does not escape them. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so different checks produce the same key: name "a_b" with an empty folder and name "a" with folder "b" both end in "_a_b_". Check treats any denial-cache hit as Allowed=false and does not consult the permission cache or the database. A deny for one pair therefore denies the other pair for 30s even when the user has that permission.

findings.title: Denial cache hides grants already reloaded into the permission cache
findings.body: A denial entry is consulted before the permission cache and before the database fallback added to see new creator permissions, and nothing deletes it when permissions are refreshed. getUserPermissions replaces the cached scope map on every reload but does not drop denial keys. After a grant, a Check for some other resource can reload permissions and observe the new scope, yet a follow-up Check for a resource denied earlier still returns Allowed=false until the denial TTL (30s) expires. That skips the requery this PR added. It also sticks when a Check runs before the creator permission is committed, including waiters on an in-flight singleflight permission fetch in getUserPermissions that started before the insert: those callers share the stale miss and then denial-cache the new dashboard or folder.

findings.title: Stale folder-tree misses are cached as denials
findings.body: When the cached scope map does not allow the resource, Check reloads permissions and calls checkPermission. Folder inheritance still uses buildFolderTree, which returns the cached tree for up to 30s and is not bypassed on this path. If the parent folder was created after that fill, the tree has no parent pointer, so an ancestor grant is not found and checkPermission returns false. Check then stores a denial for 30s. Previously, folder-cache expiry alone let the next Check rebuild the tree and allow access from the already cached ancestor scope. The denial is now served first and skips both the permission cache and a tree rebuild, so inherited access to resources in newly created folders stays denied after the folder cache is no longer stale.

findings.title: Every distinct deny reloads the full permission set
findings.body: If the denial cache misses and the cached scope map does not already allow the resource, Check always calls getIdentityPermissions. The cache short-circuit was removed from getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions, so each of those calls queries the database (plus team and basic-role lookups) inside singleflight. The denial cache only suppresses an exact repeat of the same name and folder. Sequential Checks for one user and action against different unauthorized UIDs therefore run one full permission query per resource instead of one query per user and action per TTL. Each call also inserts a denial entry keyed by the client-supplied name and folder, so a burst of distinct names grows that cache until TTL cleanup.

findings.title: Denial-cache test never sets up an allow
findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck's explicit-deny case says the permission cache allows dash1 so only the denial short-circuit can explain the deny, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false or missing scope as no permission, and the fake permission store is left empty, so the test still passes if the denial-cache lookup is removed. Nothing covers the anonymous/render key collision, underscore UID collisions, or a grant that stays denied after a permission reload.
